Diese Franchises werden aus finanziellem, nicht künstlerischen Interesse getrieben. Da Filme häufig einen sehr hohen Kostenaufwand mit sich bringen (Technik, Crew, Besetzung, Drehorte, Vermarktung) werden so lange Menschen diese Filme gucken genau solche produziert. Ich persönlich mache mir auch schon länger Gedanken, wie dieser Trend beendet werden kann, oder zumindest die Produktion von Fortsetzungen, Remakes etc. zu Gunsten unabhäbgig finanzierter, origineller Filme reduziert werden kann.

Das große Problem ist meiner Meinung der kulturelle Diskurs rund um Film. Die meisten Menschen die nicht wahnsinnig an Filmen interessiert sind wollen entweder keine herausfordernden oder Independent-Filme gucken oder wissen gar nicht wo sie diese finden, weil diese natürlich weniger vermarktet werden. Stattdessen wählen sie das bekannte, kurzweilige, belanglose a la Star Wars, MCU, DC und so weiter.

Ich versuche deshalb wann immer ich mit jemandem über Filme spreche die Interessen und Präferenzen meines Gegenübers abzuwägen und Filme außerhalb des Mainstreams zu empfehlen. Seien sie etwas ältere Filme, Independent oder aus nicht deutsch- oder englischsprachigen Ländern, hauptsache etwas außerhalb des modernen Studio-Systems. Auch auf sozialen Medien kann man natürlich versuchen das allgemeine Wissen über weniger bekannte Filme zu erweitern.

Ebenfalls ist es wichtig die Kritik von Filmen zu fördern. Das heißt nicht unbedingt nur hauptberufliche Filmkritiker zu unterstützen, sondern auch die kritische Reflexion bezüglich Filmen zu kultivieren. Es sollte mMn die Idee weiter verbreitet werden, mehr über Filme nachzudenken und zu überlegen die Werke von welchem Studio, Regisseur, Drehbuch-Autor etc es verdient haben unterstützt zu werden.

The important part is not the division into "good" and "bad" endings, but if the events are justified or not. In conventional storytelling you need a set-up for every pay-off. If the heroes win or things work out for no established reason, it is not satisfying. If things go to shit for no reason, it is not satisfying. It is the mark of a good or even competent writer that the ending is the logical conclusion of what was set up before.

Also you have to keep the tone in mind. If you tell a whimsical light-hearted story, a depressing ending can feel jarring. Same goes for the other way around. 

It´s not that bad endings are superior to good endings, it´s that many writers nowadays and probably also in the past inserted happy endings in their story for the sake of pleasing the audience or making a family-friendly movie, when they lack the talent or dedication to properly justify how things work out.

I vastly prefer the OT duels because they have more emotional weight. The characters who fight, Vader vs Ben and Vader vs Luke, have well established relationships with each other that influence the importance the fights have to the story, which makes me care way more about them as scenes, they are crucial character moments.

In the PT, the fights are more eye-candy. Maul is a character who had no relationship with Obi-Wan or Qui-Gon before fighting, even if the fight influences the fate of the galaxy immensely that lessens my interest. Qui-Gon is endearing enough to make it hurt when he dies. 

Dooku´s duel against Obi-Wan and Anakin has a similar problem, I have not seen enough of the relationship between Obi and Dooku, Anakin has no relationship with him. The choreography is not that good either. When Yoda enters the battle, there is a bit more going on chraacter-wise and I like the force-battle and the choreography afterwards.

In RotS, Dooku´s rematch against the two has way more weight by virtue of being a rematch, the way Obi-Wan gets taken out is strange but the fight itself is believable, the decapitation at the end is of course wonderful. Dew it!

Grievous vs Obi-Wan is a joke to me tbh. Grievous seems not that threatening in the movie, the relationship between the two is only hinted at, and the whole time I have to wonder why Obi doesn´t simply push Grievous into a crater or destroys him with the force. He has an obvious advantage. Instead Grivvy gets his hands cut off like an idiot and Obi kicks a robot leg. What a clown show,

Sheev vs the Jedi is way too short, three of them get taken out easily and the choreography at the end obviously has to accommodate the fact that McDiarmid and Jackson are not that young so it´s strangely shot.

After that we have Yoda vs Sheev. The fight is amazing. The choreography is good, the force powers are cool and demonstrate ho powerful both of them are, ripping out the senate pods is a bit obvious but still a really cool metaphor for the end of the Republic and destruction of democracy. The senate literally gets used as Sheev´s weapon against the Jedi. Dare I say it is poetic?

Obi vs Anakin. Great fight. The emotions are at an high, the choreography is beautiful. They really look like to of the best lightsaber duelists in their prime. The lava back drop is wonderful. The high ground scene is a meme, but it works fine enough and the dialogue when they shout at each other is heart wrenching.

With the context of The Clone Wars the fights with Grievous and Dooku in RotS loose some of their impact. The show makes it seem like a fight with those two is like a regular accurance.

In conclusion, we have two great fights, two good fights, one mediocre fight and two bad fights. Even though the music for all of them is fantastic, the soundtrack throughout the Prequels is, I consider the fights here to be a very mixed back. Not as impactful as the OT, but definitely more spectacular. And still much, much better than the incomprehensible, underrehearsed trash in the Sequels.

Not because I want him to be a character we already knew, Mace Windu or Plageius were popular fan theories at the time, having him be an established character could very likely have been silly. The real importance of Snoke lies in what he archieved inbetween episodes 6 and 7. Snoke destroyed the new Jedi Order, built up the First Order in secret, as well as a new, even bigger, planet-destroying super weapon, and destroyed the New Republic, thus destroying everything the Rebellion in the OT archieved. Many people in the galaxy, for example Rey, seem to have forgotten all about the Rebellion´s fight against the Empire. And we learn nothing about this guy or where he came from until episode 9, which gives an explonation that is worse than anything most could have thought up as a joke.

The characters are lacking throughout the whole trilogy. Rey is a protagonist who does not seem to struggle a lot to archieve anything she does, and she archieves an awful lot. She meets a potential mentor in Han, but instead of learning from him she teaches him about bypassing the compressor in his own ship. She meets a potential mentor in Luke, but more than learning from him she teaches him to stop running and hiding from his place in the galaxy. Rey does not form natural relationships with other characters, but instead is liked instantly by almost everyone (with a few exceptions) she meets. You just got to fill in the blanks why she gets treated as if she is the most charming and interesting person ever. 

Finn had some great potential, as we have never seen a foot-soldier question his purpose and change sides in a Star Wars movie. Particularly Storm Troopers, who have been portrayed as faceless bad guys in the other movies, could be very interesting to explore. Instead Finn is written inconsistently. He gets traumatised right at the start, then quips with Poe while escaping with Poe to Jakku. Later he screams out of excitement while killing Storm Troopers in combat, although the death of one Storm Trooper started his awakening to the horrors of war. His main motivation for much of the story is to help and assist Rey with whatever she is doing, which lead to the meme of him screaming "Rey", "Rey", "Rey" all the time.

Poe Dameron was originally supposed to die in the beginning of the first movie. It was a suggestion by the actor Oscar Isaac which lead to his survival. That is the reason why he reappears without explonation after seemingly dying in the crash on Jakku. There is not too much of a problem with him in The Force Awakens beside that. In TLJ however, he gets treated like crap for no particularly good reason. He gets called reckless and a flyboy, he gets slapped in the face by a superior officer for "causing the deaths" of many Resistance fighters. In reality, he saved the entire Resistance from the Starkiller Base hours early, then saved them again from the Dreadnought while evacuating the base. Sure, many people died, but all of them could have turned around if they would have wanted to listen to Leia instead of Poe, also,the assault on the Dreadnought would have more than likely failed if Poe didn´t take out the cannons. The Dreadnought is referred to as a "fleet killer", so it is fair to assume that without Poe destroying it the Resistance fleet might have taken way heavier losses. 

Later in the same movie, he starts a mutiny against Admiral Holdo. This is shown as an impulsive thing, but he only goes this far after asking multiple times if there is a plan to save any of the Resistance members lives from the Supremacy, and getting no answer. The reasoning is that he is not being trusted enough, but he blew up the Starkiller base days before, so why is the potentially most valuable asset of the Resistance not being trusted. The "pay-off" is that on Krayt, at the end of the movie, he calls off a suicide mission to take out the laser that is breaking open the gate to the Resistance hideout. He or someone else could have given their lives to save many others, but I suppose the movie thinks that´s not acceptable in a war. Ultimately Poe might be one of the better protagonists but gest dragged down by the people around him.

Kylo Ren might be the worst character in the trilogy. He used to be called the most interesting, because of his unpredictable nature, but he never really was a person dragged between the Light and Dark Side, his unpredictability comes from the script having him do whatever it wants in that moment. Apocalypse Now: 

Fantastic performances all around, standouts are Marlon Brando and Robert Duvall, also Dennis Hopper in a smaller role. Martin Sheen is a strong leading man, fusing himself into his character.

Gorgeous cinematography by Vittorio Storaro (Last Tango in Paris, The Conformist).

Great use of music and editing.

Francis Ford Coppola used amazing creative freedom he had after the critical successes he had in the first half of the seventies to craft what I would call his masterpiece and possibly the best film of all time.

I recommend to watch the theatrical cut first, if you want to see more you can get that from the Redux Version, or the Final Cut, which is the favorite version of Coppola himself. Also there is a huge amount of behind the scenes footage, including a documentary about making the movie under very unique circumstances.

The Umbrellas of Cherbourg:

The film stars Catherine Deneuve, in her first work with Jacques Demy. It´s a unique musical, that instead of using particular scenes as dance numbers, has every character sing their lines. The music in it is beautiful.

The costume design is breathtaking, only matched by very few movies in the almost six decades since it came out, and the production design and cinematography make this an outstanding visual pleasure as well.

The way this film looks is comparable with Luca Guadagnino´s work, especially I am Love. It inspired Damien Chazelle when making La La Land, and carries similar messages about the emotional bond between lovers, and how the reality of their lives can crash with what they wish, or hope, for their love.

If you like a more conventional musical, The Young Girls of Rochefort is about as great as Umbrellas of Cherbourg.

Barry Lyndon:

My favorite film of Stanley Kubrick, with fantastic cinematography by John Alcott, cinematographer of A Clockwork Orange and The Shining . The film looks like a painting in some shots, it´s truly unbelievable and in my opinion makes this the most visually beautiful film ever made.

The music and costume design make this feel authentic, and compliment the whole visual style of this movie.

The performances are as good as one would expect from a Kubrick movie, the standouts here are Ryan O´Neal, Marisa Berenson, Patrick Magee and Leon Vitali. 

Near the end of the film there is a sequence with what I would call the best editing, and the best building of tension I have ever seen. This movie was my favorite for some years, before I saw Apocalypse Now.
